title: Burning since childhood

clues.t: 32-year-old man with burning pain in his hands and feet since he was a boy.
It's worse in heat, with fever, or during exercise. He barely sweats.
Clusters of tiny dark red spots around his navel and swimwear area.
Urine dipstick: protein 2+
His uncle had kidney failure and a stroke in his 40s.
Eye exam: whorl-like patterns in both corneas

pearl: An X-linked lysosomal storage disease. Women can be affected too, often more mildly. Childhood burning pain plus reduced sweating is a classic early clue. Enzyme replacement and oral therapies exist, so diagnosis matters.

title: Moon face, thin skin

clues.t: 41-year-old woman, gained 12 kg mostly around her middle.
Struggles to get up from a low chair.
Bruises with minor knocks. Skin feels thin.
Wide purple stretch marks on her abdomen.
New hypertension and fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L
1 mg overnight dexamethasone test: 9 am cortisol 310 nmol/L

pearl: Exogenous steroids are the commonest cause, so ask about creams, inhalers, joint injections and supplements. Proximal weakness, easy bruising and wide purple striae are the most discriminating signs.

title: Heavy lids by dinner

clues.t: 34-year-old woman with double vision when reading at night.
Her left eyelid droops by evening. Fine in the morning.
Jaw gets tired chewing steak.
Pupils normal. No pain. No headache.
An ice pack on the eyelid for 2 minutes clearly lifts the droop.
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies positive

pearl: Fatigability is the key feature, so examine with sustained upgaze. About half of purely ocular cases are antibody-negative. Order a CT chest to look for thymoma.

title: Wetland weekend

clues.t: 45-year-old woman with painful, stiff hands, wrists and ankles.
Exhausted. Struggling to open jars for 3 weeks.
A faint red rash on her trunk came and went in the first week.
Low-grade fever at the start. No history of joint problems.
Went camping near coastal wetlands in late summer and was bitten a lot.
Alphavirus IgM positive, IgG rising on repeat serology

pearl: Australia's commonest mosquito-borne infection. Symptoms can last months. Confirm with paired serology, as a single IgM is often a false positive. Treatment is supportive; it's notifiable in NSW.

title: The cat is sleepy too

clues.t: 35-year-old woman with headaches and nausea for 2 weeks.
Worse at home in the evenings, better at work.
Her wife and their son have similar headaches.
The family cat has been unusually lethargic.
SpO₂ 99% on room air.
They started using an old gas space heater this month.

pearl: Pulse oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated, so a normal SpO₂ is falsely reassuring. Order a venous COHb, and always ask whether others at home are unwell.

title: The renovator

clues.t: 38-year-old man with crampy abdominal pain and constipation for 2 months.
Irritable and forgetful. His partner says he's "not himself".
Hb 104 g/L, microcytic, but ferritin is normal
Blood film: basophilic stippling of red cells
He's been restoring a 1920s Newcastle terrace on weekends.
He dry-sands the old paint with no mask.

pearl: Australian homes built before 1970 often contain lead paint. NHMRC advises investigating a blood lead level above 5 µg/dL. Ask about hobbies and renovations, and check the whole household, especially children.

title: Straight edges

clues.t: 62-year-old woman with a dry cough and breathlessness for 2 weeks.
Low-grade fevers. Two courses of antibiotics haven't helped.
She finished treatment for right breast cancer 8 weeks ago.
Fine crackles over the right upper chest only. Oxygen saturation 94% on room air.
Chest X-ray: hazy right upper zone shadowing with an oddly straight edge
CT: ground-glass change matching the shape of her radiotherapy field, ignoring the lobe boundaries

pearl: Radiation pneumonitis usually appears 1 to 6 months after chest radiotherapy. The clue is a shadow that follows the beam, not the anatomy. Medical physicists plan every beam to keep lung dose low, which is why it's uncommon. Mild cases settle on their own; more troublesome ones usually respond to steroids.

title: Mirror image

clues.t: 34-year-old man with a wet cough he says he's had 'since forever'.
Blocked nose and sinus infections since childhood. Grommets twice as a kid.
He and his partner have been trying for a baby for 3 years.
Semen analysis: normal count, but the sperm barely move
CT chest: bronchiectasis in both lower lobes
Chest X-ray: heart and stomach bubble on the right. The radiographer re-checked the side marker.

pearl: Primary ciliary dyskinesia: cilia that can't beat properly cause a lifelong wet cough, sinusitis and bronchiectasis, and the same fault slows sperm. About half of people with it have their organs mirror-flipped (situs inversus), which makes it Kartagener syndrome. Always check the side marker before calling dextrocardia. Happy International Day of Radiology.

title: Prawns and regret

clues.t: 58-year-old man woke at 3 am with a screaming pain in his foot.
The base of his big toe is red, hot and swollen. Even the bedsheet hurts.
Boxing Day. He had prawns, ham and "a few" beers yesterday.
He started a fluid tablet for his blood pressure last month.
Serum urate 0.38 mmol/L (upper normal)
Joint aspirate: needle-shaped crystals, negatively birefringent

pearl: Urate can be normal during a flare, so a normal level doesn't rule gout out. Thiazide diuretics raise urate. Joint aspiration showing crystals is the gold standard. Gout is especially common in Māori and Pacific men, largely because of inherited differences in how the body clears urate. It's not just the prawns.

title: One-sided story

clues.t: 71-year-old woman with burning pain around the right side of her chest for 3 days.
ECG and troponin are normal.
The pain stops exactly at the midline, front and back.
Her skin there is exquisitely tender to light touch.
Today, clusters of small blisters on a red base have appeared in a band.
She had chickenpox as a child.

pearl: Pain often comes 2–3 days before the rash. Start antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset. A blister on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) means the eye may be involved: refer urgently.

title: Ring doesn't fit

clues.t: 48-year-old man, sweating more than ever.
Partner says his snoring is now unbearable.
Had his wedding ring resized twice. Shoe size went up one.
Gaps have appeared between his lower teeth.
Carpal tunnel symptoms in both hands, new hypertension.
IGF-1 three times the upper limit of normal

pearl: Changes are so slow that family often miss them, so compare old photos. IGF-1 is the screening test; confirm with GH failing to suppress on a glucose tolerance test, then pituitary MRI.

title: New habits

clues.t: 21-year-old man, fit and well, with 4 days of fever, dry cough and pain on deep breaths.
He's now breathless walking to the bathroom. SpO2 87% on room air.
Chest X-ray: bilateral hazy shadows and small effusions. Two days of IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin haven't touched it.
Full blood count: neutrophils up, eosinophils normal. Influenza, COVID-19 and Legionella tests negative.
Three weeks ago, on a gap-year trip, he started smoking for the first time.
Bronchoalveolar lavage: 42% eosinophils. Cultures sterile.

pearl: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia can follow taking up smoking (or a big change in smoking or vaping habits) within weeks. It looks like severe atypical pneumonia or ARDS, and blood eosinophils are often normal at first, so the answer hides in the lavage. It responds fast to steroids and rarely comes back if the trigger stops. Happy World Pneumonia Day.

title: Wet, wobbly, wacky

clues.t: 74-year-old man whose walking has slowly changed over a year.
Short, shuffling steps. His feet look glued to the floor.
Now he can't always make it to the toilet in time.
His wife says he's become slow and vague.
No tremor. Arms swing normally.
CT: enlarged ventricles out of proportion to brain shrinkage

pearl: Gait problems, incontinence and confusion together form the classic triad. Gait usually comes first. A large-volume lumbar puncture that improves walking predicts benefit from a shunt. It's one of the few reversible causes of cognitive decline.

title: Runs in the family
accept: maturity onset diabetes of the young

clues.t: 24-year-old woman, slim and well. A work health check flagged a high fasting glucose.
HbA1c 51 mmol/mol · BMI 22 · No ketones
Her mum was diagnosed at 25 and her grandfather at 30. Both were told 'type 2'. Neither was overweight.
GAD and IA-2 antibodies negative · C-peptide normal
Her urine dipstick shows glucose even when her blood glucose is only mildly raised.
Genetic testing: HNF1A variant

pearl: Monogenic diabetes, passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. Think of it when diabetes appears before about 35 in generation after generation, without antibodies and with C-peptide preserved. It's often mislabelled as type 1 or type 2, and getting the label right changes management and family testing. Happy World Diabetes Day, and happy birthday, Frederick Banting.

title: Still open

clues.t: Baby girl born at 27 weeks, now 5 days old in the NICU.
She'd been improving, but now needs more breathing support again.
Her pulses feel unusually bounding, even in her palms.
A new murmur at the upper left sternal edge.
Echo: blood shunting left to right, from the aorta into the pulmonary artery

pearl: The ductus arteriosus usually closes within days of birth. In very premature babies it often stays open, so extra blood floods the lungs and runs off from the body: bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure are the clues. Many close on their own; the NICU team decides whether it needs help. Happy World Prematurity Day to every early arrival and their families.

title: Turned down to low

clues.t: 44-year-old woman, tired all the time and gaining weight without eating more.
Always cold. Wears a cardigan in January.
Constipated. Dry skin. Her hair is coming out in the shower.
Her ankle reflexes relax slowly after the tap.
Her mother takes "a little pill for her neck".
TSH 28 mIU/L · free T4 low

pearl: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the commonest cause in Australia. Lithium and amiodarone can cause it too. Recheck TSH about 6 weeks after any dose change.

title: Overdue
accept: squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix

clues.t: 46-year-old woman with bleeding after sex for 3 months.
Also spotting between periods. Her cycles used to be like clockwork.
Her last screening test was 'probably 15 years ago'. Life got busy.
She left school before the HPV vaccine program began.
Speculum exam: an irregular lesion on the cervix that bleeds on touch.
HPV 16 detected

pearl: Almost all cervical cancers are caused by HPV, and most are found in people who are under-screened or never screened. Bleeding after sex always deserves a look. In Australia the Cervical Screening Test, which can be self-collected, is for women and people with a cervix aged 25 to 74, every 5 years. Self-collection is helping reach people who screen less, including many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and LGBTIQA+ people. Australia aims to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem by 2035.

title: Out of puff

clues.t: 63-year-old man, breathless walking up the hill to the shops.
A phlegmy cough most mornings for years. 'Just a smoker's cough,' he says.
Three chest infections in the last two winters.
Smoked 30 a day from 16 until 58.
Barrel chest. Quiet breath sounds. Long, wheezy breaths out.
Spirometry after a puffer: FEV1/FVC 0.55

pearl: Airflow limitation that doesn't fully reverse: FEV1/FVC stays below 0.7 after a bronchodilator. Smoking is the main cause in Australia; worldwide, smoke from cooking and heating fuels matters too. Spirometry makes the diagnosis, a stethoscope can't. Happy World COPD Day, and welcome to World AMR Awareness Week.

title: The three Ps

clues.t: 44-year-old woman with attacks of pounding headache.
She drenches her shirt with sweat during each one.
Heart races and he feels a sense of doom. Episodes last 20 minutes.
BP between episodes is normal.
BP during an episode measured at the pharmacy: 210/120
Plasma free metanephrines markedly raised

pearl: Headache, sweating and palpitations together are the classic triad. Never start a beta-blocker before an alpha-blocker, as unopposed alpha stimulation can trigger a hypertensive crisis. About a third are hereditary.

title: Cream crackers

clues.t: 52-year-old woman whose eyes feel gritty, like sand under the lids.
She can't eat a dry cracker without a glass of water.
Her dentist found five new cavities this year.
Both cheeks near her jaw are swollen and puffy.
Aching joints. Tired all the time.
Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies positive

pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth is the core of it. Schirmer's test measures tear production. Lymphoma risk is raised, so a persistently enlarged parotid gland needs review.
